accuracy.evidence: Checked against AQA GCSE Combined Science 4.1.1.3 (development of the model of the atom: plum pudding, alpha scattering, nuclear model, Bohr shells, protons, Chadwick 1932) and OpenStax Chemistry 2e section 2.2. Dates verified: Dalton 1803, Thomson electron 1897, Geiger-Marsden from 1909, Rutherford 1911, Bohr 1913, Chadwick 1932; about 1 in 8000 reflected is Geiger and Marsden's 1909 figure; electron mass about 1/7300 of an alpha, stated as about 8000 times lighter.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented GCSE slips: particles going through gaps between atoms (challenge tag gaps), electrons causing the deflections (tag electron, m9), spread-out pudding charge causing bounces (tag pudding), muddling model order (timeline step plus tag order), crediting Bohr with the neutron (tag chad), and the view that replaced models were just wrong or old (tags old, whim, adult text on evidence of its time).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagfoil is a new mechanic: a five-slot model timeline with drawn model glyphs, a live gold-foil scattering simulator that integrates inverse-square repulsion for each alpha particle and tallies straight, deflected and back-scattered paths, a zoomed aim-and-fire nucleus target, and an evidence-to-idea matcher. No existing lab simulates Rutherford scattering.

lab_teaches.evidence: The steps follow the GCSE story in order: models change with evidence (timeline with the reason for each change), the plum pudding prediction against the real spray (about 85 percent straight, 13 percent deflected, 1 percent back in the sim), the need for a tiny dense positive nucleus (only a near-centre aim turns past 90 degrees), and the six discoveries that forced each change.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions are each tested straight away: why models change before the timeline, the plum pudding forecast before firing 40 particles, what could turn a particle round (nucleus, pudding or electrons) before the aim task, and which model explained hydrogen's exact colours before the evidence matcher.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge items rotate answer order and every distractor is tagged (gaps, small, pudding, electron, order, chad, old, whim, thom, dalton) with its own explanation, e.g. Electrons are about 8000 times lighter than an alpha particle. In the lab, wrong timeline cards explain what must come first and missed aims report the turn angle in degrees.

readability.evidence: Student text scores about FK 4.3 and adult text about FK 7.1, inside the learner targets. GCSE terms are used exactly and defined in context: model, electron, plum pudding model, alpha particle, nucleus, nuclear model, shells or energy levels, proton, neutron, with sentences kept short.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph advances the evidence chain: why models exist, Dalton to Thomson, the scattering result and its meaning, Bohr, protons and Chadwick. The adult text names the specification, the experiment detail, a common mistakes list and the lab sequence. Items use parameterised bounce counts, scale-model sizes and neutron counts.

mobile.evidence: Checked at iPhone 13 (390px) light and Android 360px dark: five timeline slots and a 3-column tray fit, the foil sim and tally line stay readable, the zoomed aim line and nucleus are clear, and the six evidence tiles stack without clipping. Fire, Up, Down and tray buttons wrap below the canvas as large tap targets.

accessibility.evidence: Every gesture has a button twin (tray cards, Fire 1 and Fire 10, Up, Down and Fire, evidence buttons). The live status and canvas aria-label speak each placement with its year and reason, the running tally, aim percent and turn angle; axe ran clean in both themes; path colours are backed by the text tally.
